newsitem.title: PERU: FEATURE-Peru hostage crisis recalls horror of People's Jails.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Peru hostage crisis recalls horror of People's Jails.

text.p: David Ballon Vera weighed 220 pounds (100 kg) on Sept. 11, 1992, the day he was abducted.

His body was found six months later dumped on the side of a Lima street with a bullet hole in his head. It was clear he had been starved and mistreated in the months before he was killed when he was held incommunicado in a damp six-by-six foot (two-by-two-metre) closet, watched night and day, as anguished family members tried to negotiate his freedom.

"When they abandoned his body, after giving him the coup de grace, my brother weighed 47 kilos (100 pounds)," Efrain Ballon Vera said. "They didn't kill him in one day. They did it slowly over six months during which he suffered every day."

His kidnappers were guerrillas of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA), whose members are holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home and demanding the release of 400 jailed comrades they complain are suffering from inhuman prison conditions.

Human rights groups also have criticised harsh prison conditions for rebels in Peru. But those complaints ring hollow for about 30 businessmen and others held in MRTA "Carceles del Pueblo" (People's Jails) in the late 1980s and early 1990s and for their relatives.

The Cuban-inspired guerrilla group rose up against the state in 1984 and was initially viewed as a Robin Hood-like group that robbed from the rich to give to the poor. But, eclipsed by the larger Shining Path and under pressure from security forces, it increasingly resorted to bank robbery, kidnapping, extortion and protection for drug traffickers.
WEALTHY BUSINESSMEN ABDUCTED
Those singled out for abduction were usually successful businessmen able to pay ransoms of up to $100,000. The MRTA rented houses and built secret rooms in basements and closets to be used as cells.
Among the early victims was poultry magnate Julio Ikeda, kidnapped on Sept. 26, 1987. "It was like a tomb," Peru's "Chicken King" said. "I barely had room to stand up."

He was fed three glasses of milk, a piece of bread and a banana each day. "Once, as punishment, I wasn't given anything for three days," said Ikeda, who was freed after two months when his family paid the ransom.

Retired Air Force Gen. Hector Jeri Garcia was abducted as he arrived for work on July 7, 1988, by eight men who smashed in his car window and pulled him out. Jeri's family was sent photos of him sitting in front of a red-and-white MRTA flag, a masked rebel at each shoulder.
When negotiations stalled, the MRTA bombed his home. He was freed 3-1/2 months later after his family paid a ransom and distributed 7,000 food baskets to the poor.

The 17 years of guerrilla wars unleashed by Shining Path and the MRTA have cost 30,000 lives and $25 billion in economic damage. Violence has waned since the 1992 capture of rebel chiefs, but Peru's prisons are packed with some 5,000 people charged with treason or terrorism, hundreds of whom human rights groups believe to be innocent. Many have suffered torture and their prison regime is harsh by any standards.
Prisoners spend 23-1/2 hours a day in crowded, dimly lit cells with 30 minutes a day in the exercise yard and one half-hour visit a month by a family member.
SLOW DEATH IN 'TOMBS'

Families complain their loved ones are suffering a slow death in virtual "tombs." Since the Japanese Embassy siege began on Dec. 17, conditions have become worse and visits have been banned. But the rebels' relatives dismiss any comparison with People's Jails.
"The MRTA did not physically mistreat prisoners," the wife of one jailed rebel said. "There were some excesses but they were isolated cases and the MRTA punished those responsible."

She called the MRTA's kidnap victims "exploiters of the people" and said abuses occured only if families contacted police or refused to "pay the war tax," which is what the rebels call their ransom demands.

The MRTA's spokesman in Europe, Isaac Velazco, denied the group has mistreated prisoners and said it abides by the Geneva Convention on treatment of prisoners of war, despite lacking the prison infrastructure of the state. "No prisoner of war in the hands of the MRTA was mistreated, tortured or abused. None has criticised the conditions of our hospitality," he told Peruvian television.

One foreign aid worker said state prisons and MRTA jails cannot be compared because "you expect more from the state." But that is little consolation for those whose family members languished in People's Jails.

Jailed guerrillas "are guaranteed everything," Efrain Ballon said. "They have human rights groups at hand, someone to complain to. But the people held in jails run by these gentlemen, who could they complain to?"
